Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I distract myself with something else
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Threat.value: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
I only feel safe in a very limited number of places

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

vignette: Thirty years ago, fleeing across a porous border meant trading one kind of terror for another. At the checkpoint, the guards never warned them; they simply roared orders, their voices cracking through the damp morning air. When David Weiss stepped too close to a metal detector, a guard backhanded him without hesitation, the cold barrel of a rifle pressing hard against his ribs. He learned quickly that sudden hands and raised voices meant imminent violence, a visceral association that never faded. In the years that followed, his body never forgave that morning. He came to believe his own nervous system was a traitor, firing alarm signals long after the border fences were gone. This conviction tightened his grip on the world: he stopped relying on his own judgment, certain that someone else should have stopped the soldiers, or that he had simply failed to navigate the crossing correctly. Because he couldn't trust his instincts, his attention fractured during sermons, and he became compulsive about where he sat in the sanctuary. He only felt secure in a few specific pews near the back wall, and when he couldn't find them, the fear of exposure took over. Now, at sixty-three, David’s life as a community rabbi is structured around these quiet compensations. During morning minyan, he always scans the room first, mapping sightlines to the door before choosing his place on the bimah. When a parishioner reaches out to hug him during the peaceable greeting, David stiffens, the sudden contact pulling him straight back to the checkpoint. The tactile shock feeds his self-reproach; he tells himself he deserves the discomfort for remaining so jumpy, and immediately retreats behind distraction, focusing intensely on the prayer book until the tremors pass. His punishment thinking deepens his sense of helplessness, which in turn amplifies his physical hyperarousal. He stops trusting his own safety perceptions, and that erosion of trust makes him hypersensitive to the next shout or sight of steel. The loop tightened over the decades. Because his body continued to signal danger in the sanctuary, David avoided leaning into his partner’s presence, fearing that emotional closeness would leave him exposed to the same helplessness he felt at the border. His withdrawal only confirmed his belief that he was fundamentally incapable of protecting himself. Unable to self-soothe, he began to anticipate threats where there were none, his attention constantly fracturing toward exits and shadows. This hyper-vigilance made him interpret a raised voice at the market or a glint of metal on a shelf as imminent attacks, which reliably triggered his startle response and sent him into avoidance rituals. His avoidance of emotional contact then reinforced his conviction that he could never rely on himself, ensuring his body remained locked in fight-or-flight, which inevitably summoned the next wave of triggers in his daily life. His partner finally sat him down three weeks ago, noting how he no longer slept in their shared bed and how he flinched whenever she reached for his hand. David came to counseling hoping to quiet the internal sirens, terrified that the synagogue would lose its spiritual leader, and desperate to prove he wasn’t broken, just trapped. He arrived at the therapist’s office with a notebook full of avoided appointments and a quiet dread that the very space might trigger another evacuation. He wanted to believe he could finally trust himself again, and that the sanctuary could once again be a place of rest rather than a perimeter to be guarded.
